title: Fractions & Decimals
weightage: High — fractions and decimals thread through ratios, percents, algebra and Data Interpretation
intro: Fractions are where careful GRE test-takers separate from careless ones. The basic on-screen calculator handles decimals, but it will happily give you 0.6666666667 for 2/3 and then you have lost the exactness the question wanted — so the smart move is to stay in fractions as long as possible and convert only at the end. A fraction is just a division waiting to happen, and every fraction, decimal and percent is the same value in three outfits. This chapter drills the fluency the test assumes: simplifying, comparing without a calculator, the four operations, decimal place value, and the conversions that let you switch outfits instantly. Get comfortable here and ratios, percents and even algebra stop feeling like new topics.

items.name: Simplify
items.formula: divide top and bottom by their GCD

items.name: Cross-multiply to compare
items.formula: a/b vs c/d ⇒ compare ad vs bc

topics.name: Equivalent Fractions & Simplifying
topics.details: Two fractions are equivalent when they represent the same value: 2/3, 4/6 and 6/9 are all one point on the number line. You generate equivalents by multiplying (or dividing) top and bottom by the same nonzero number — that keeps the value because you are multiplying by a disguised 1. To simplify (reduce to lowest terms), divide the numerator and denominator by their GCD; a fraction is fully reduced when the two are coprime. On the GRE this matters for speed and for matching answer choices, which are usually given in lowest terms. It also drives Quantitative Comparison: to compare 12/18 with 2/3 you do not need a calculator — reduce 12/18 to 2/3 and see they are equal. Always simplify before you compute; smaller numbers mean fewer slips.

solved.solution: GCD(18, 24) = 6. Divide both by 6: 18/24 = 3/4.
The denominator went from 5 to 45, a ×9. Apply the same to the top: 3 × 9 = 27. So 3/5 = 27/45.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 15/25. Quantity B: 3/5. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Reduce 15/25 by GCD 5 → 3/5. Quantity A = Quantity B; they are equal.

topics.name: Comparing Fractions
topics.details: Comparing fractions quickly is a core GRE skill, especially in Quantitative Comparison where the whole question is "which is bigger?". Three tools cover almost everything. (1) Cross-multiplication: for positive fractions, a/b vs c/d reduces to comparing a·d with b·c — bigger cross-product sits over the bigger fraction. (2) Common numerator: if the tops match, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger (1/4 > 1/5). (3) Benchmarks: compare each to 1/2 or 1 to sort them at a glance — 5/9 is just over 1/2, 4/9 just under. Watch two traps: cross-multiplication's direction flips if a fraction is negative, and a fraction greater than 1 (like 7/6) beats any proper fraction outright. Reaching for the calculator to compare fractions is usually slower and can hide ties.

solved.solution: Cross-multiply: 3×9 = 27 and 7×4 = 28. Since 28 > 27, the fraction over 28 — that is 4/9 — is greater.
As decimals (or via benchmarks near 0.6): 3/5 = 0.60, 5/8 = 0.625, 2/3 ≈ 0.667. Least to greatest: 3/5, 5/8, 2/3.
Cross-multiply: 5×8 = 40 and 6×7 = 42. 42 > 40, so 7/8 (over 42) is larger.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 7/12. Quantity B: 1/2. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Benchmark against 1/2 = 6/12. Since 7/12 > 6/12, Quantity A is greater.

topics.name: Operations with Fractions
topics.details: The four operations each have their own rule. To add or subtract, you need a common denominator, then combine the numerators (the LCM of the denominators keeps numbers smallest). To multiply, go straight across — numerator × numerator over denominator × denominator — and cancel common factors before multiplying to keep it clean: (3/4)(8/9) becomes (3/4)(8/9) → cancel 3 with 9 and 8 with 4 → (1/1)(2/3) = 2/3. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b)(d/c). Mixed numbers should be converted to improper fractions first (2¾ = 11/4) so the rules apply cleanly. The recurring GRE insight: staying in fractions gives exact answers, while the basic calculator forces you into rounded decimals that can cost you a "which is greater" call.

solved.solution: Common denominator 12: 2/3 = 8/12, 1/4 = 3/12. Sum = 11/12.
Cancel first: 3 and 9 share 3 → 1 and 3; 8 and 4 share 4 → 2 and 1. Left with (1/1)(2/3) = 2/3.
Multiply by the reciprocal: (5/6)(3/10) = 15/60 = 1/4.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6. Quantity B: 1. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Common denominator 6: 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1. Quantity A = Quantity B; they are equal.

unsolved.problem: Compute 2¼ + 1½ as an improper fraction, then simplify.

topics.name: Decimals & Place Value
topics.details: A decimal is a fraction whose denominator is a power of 10, and the position of each digit names that power: tenths, hundredths, thousandths, and so on. So 0.47 is 47/100, and 0.005 is 5/1000. Reading place value cleanly makes rounding and estimation reliable: to round 3.147 to the hundredths place, look at the next digit (7 ≥ 5) and round up to 3.15. Multiplying or dividing by powers of 10 just slides the decimal point — ×100 moves it two places right, ÷1000 moves it three left. When you multiply two decimals, count the total decimal places in the factors and put that many in the answer (0.3 × 0.04 = 0.012, three places). The GRE uses decimals heavily in Data Interpretation and money contexts, and a misplaced decimal point is one of the most common careless errors — say the place value out loud when it matters.

solved.problem: What is the digit in the hundredths place of 27.384?
solved.solution: Places after the point: 3 is tenths, 8 is hundredths, 4 is thousandths. The hundredths digit is 8.
Hundredths digit is 6; the next digit is 8 (≥ 5), so round up: 4.27.
Multiply 6 × 5 = 30; total decimal places 1 + 2 = 3, so place the point three from the right: 0.030 = 0.03.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 0.4. Quantity B: 0.400. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Trailing zeros do not change value: 0.400 = 0.4. Quantity A = Quantity B; they are equal.

unsolved.problem: What digit is in the thousandths place of 5.9174?

topics.name: Fraction–Decimal–Percent Conversions
topics.details: Fractions, decimals and percents are three names for one value, and fluent conversion is one of the highest-leverage GRE skills. Fraction → decimal: divide top by bottom. Decimal → percent: multiply by 100 (shift the point two places right). Percent → fraction: put it over 100 and reduce (25% = 25/100 = 1/4). The real time-saver is memorising the benchmark table so you recognise values on sight: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/3 ≈ 0.333 ≈ 33.3%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5%, 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%, 2/3 ≈ 0.667 ≈ 66.7%. With that table, "62.5% of 240" becomes (5/8)×240 = 150 in one step, no calculator. Knowing which fractions give terminating decimals (only denominators of the form 2^a·5^b, in lowest terms) also lets you predict a clean vs repeating result before dividing.

solved.problem: Convert 5/8 to a decimal and a percent.
Convert 0.35 to a fraction in lowest terms.
Convert 175% to a fraction and a decimal.
Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 3/8. Quantity B: 0.38. Which is greater?
solved.solution: 3/8 = 0.375. Compare with 0.38: 0.375 < 0.380, so Quantity B is greater.

unsolved.problem: Convert 0.24 to a fraction in lowest terms.
Convert 120% to a fraction in lowest terms.

shortcuts: Stay in fractions for exact answers; convert to a decimal only at the very end. The basic calculator rounds and can hide ties.
Memorise the benchmark table (1/8 = 12.5%, 3/8 = 37.5%, 1/3 ≈ 33.3%, …). It turns "37.5% of 64" into (3/8)×64 = 24 instantly.
Compare two positive fractions by cross-multiplying: bigger cross-product sits over the bigger fraction.
Cancel common factors BEFORE multiplying fractions — you work with far smaller numbers and rarely need to simplify at the end.
A fraction terminates as a decimal only if, in lowest terms, its denominator is 2^a·5^b. Otherwise it repeats.
To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers and place the point using the total count of decimal places.
mistakes: Adding fractions straight across (2/3 + 1/4 ≠ 3/7). You must find a common denominator first.
Trusting a rounded calculator decimal on a "which is greater?" call — 0.6667 vs 2/3 can flip the answer.
Forgetting to invert the second fraction when dividing (multiply by the reciprocal, not the fraction).
Misplacing the decimal point when multiplying decimals — miscounting the total decimal places.
Leaving an answer unreduced when the choices are in lowest terms, then failing to find the match.
Comparing decimals digit-count first (thinking 0.089 > 0.1 because it has more digits).

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — Quantity A: 5/9. Quantity B: 0.55. Which is greater?
pyq.a: 5/9 ≈ 0.5556 > 0.55, so Quantity A is greater. Repeating decimals just past a benchmark are a classic trap.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry (fraction box) — 3/4 of a class of 32 study Spanish. Enter the number of students as a fraction of the whole reduced, then the count.
pyq.a: (3/4)×32 = 24 students; as a fraction of the class that is 24/32 = 3/4.

pyq.q: A recipe uses 2/3 cup of sugar; you make 1½ batches. How much sugar as a fraction?
pyq.a: (2/3)×(3/2) = 1 cup exactly — the fractions cancel cleanly, which is why staying in fractions beats decimals here.

summary: A fraction is a division and a decimal is a fraction over a power of 10 — the same value in different outfits.
Simplify with the GCD; a fraction is fully reduced when numerator and denominator are coprime.
Compare positive fractions by cross-multiplying or by benchmarking against 1/2 and 1.
Add/subtract need a common denominator; multiply straight across (cancel first); divide by the reciprocal.
Place value governs rounding and decimal multiplication — count total decimal places for products.
Convert fluently: fraction→decimal by dividing, decimal→percent by ×100, percent→fraction over 100.
Memorise the benchmark table so common values are recognised on sight.
Stay in fractions for exactness; the basic calculator rounds and can flip close comparisons.
